Syed Mahmudul Ahsan, Advocate ------- For the Petitioner.

parties:
Kazi Mamnur Rashid ------- Petitioner 
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mamnoon Rahman J : In an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the revised Electoral Roll prepared by the respondents for the general election scheduled to be held on 22 January, 2007 should not be declared inconsistent with the provisions of the Representation of the People Order 1972 and the directives passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 54 and 55 of 2006 and also to show cause as to why the respondents should not be directed to prepare an Electoral Roll strictly as per the directives of the Appellate Division and as well as following the provisions of law and also, why they should not be directed to issue voter identification cards and prepare transparent ballot boxes for all the future elections of the country. 

 2. The short facts relevant for the disposal of this Rule are; The petitioner is a law abiding citizen of the country and a voter under a constituency. On 6-8-2005, the respondents took decision to prepare a new and fresh voter list. Challenging the same 2 (two) writ petitions, namely. Writ Petition Nos. 9157 and 9180 of 2005 have been preferred before the High Court Division. After hearing the cases, the High Court Division disposed of them with some directions regarding change, alteration and modification of the voter list. Being aggrieved by the said order passed by the High Court Division, the respondents preferred Civil Appeal being Nos. 54 and 55 of 2006 before the Appellate Division. After hearing the parties, the Appellate Division dismissed the appeal with modifications of the High Court Division's judgments. Thereafter, the respondents prepared a revised Electoral Roll for the ensuing election scheduled to be held on 22-1-2007. But the said Electoral Roll was erroneous and not prepared according to the Electoral Roll Ordinance 1982, the relevant Rules and the specific directives passed by the Appellate Division in the appeals mentioned above. While addressing the nation on 11-1-2007, the President of the Republic admits such discrepancies in the voter lists. The Election Commission being an independent body is to hold any election in a fair and free manner so the choice and mind of the people should be reflected properly. The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh empowers the Election Commission to do all necessary function in this regard. The Election Commission is armed with sufficient laws for holding election independently but because of administrative interference in the affairs of the Election Commission from its very inception, it could not perform its functions independently and judicially resulting in non holding of free and fair elections time to time. The provision for introduction of appropriate ballot box is available in the law, namely, Representation of the People Order, 1972 but the Election Commission has failed to take appropriate steps for preparation of such boxes, which is a sine qua non for holding a free and fair election, The Election Commission is under legal obligation to comply with and follow all the laws related to election as well as the provisions of the Constitution of the Republic, but owing to administrative interference by the other organs of the State and because of the Rules of Business 1996, lack of infrastructures and manpower the Election Commission has failed to achieve its desired goal since independence. In the Representation of People the Order, 1972 there is a provision for preparation of voter ID card but subsequently, that provision has been stayed by Act XIII of 1996 and the Election Commission failed to take any initiative to remove the legal barriers. For the aforesaid reasons, the Election Commission has miserably failed to ensure the free will of the people who are the main source of power as mentioned in Article 7 of the Constitution of the Republic. The present electoral system is a defective one and has become obsolete and any election under the said system will not ensure the main purpose of the Constitution of the Republic that a Government is to be elected through a free, fair and credible election reflecting the supreme wish of the people. 

 3. Respondent Nos.1 and 3 entered appearance by filing affidavit-in-opposition. The case of respondent Nos. 1 and 3 is that the statements made in the writ petition are misleading and contrary to the actual state of affairs. The respondents have already taken initiative to prepare the Electoral Roll as per law and steps were taken for preparation of ballot boxes. The provisions for introduction of voter identification cards remain suspended by a law, namely Act of 1996. The Election Commission, however, its considering the introduction of voter identification by removing the legal barriers. 

 4. Mr Syed Mahmudul Ahsan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, placed the relevant provisions of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh regarding election, the composition and functions of the Election Commission and the provisions of Representation of the People Order, 1972 and the Rules made thereunder, the Electoral Roll Ordinance 1982, the Rules made thereunder, the Conduct of the Election Rules, 1972, the Act XIII of 1996 and Code of Conduct Rules enacted by the Commission exercising the power conferred by Article 91 (b) of the Representation of the People Order, 1972. He submits that as per the Representation of the People Order 1972 and Electoral Roll Ordinance 1982 the Election Commission is under legal obligation to upgrade the voter list time to time applying all modern methods and the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 54 and 55 both of 2007 confirmed the procedures to be followed and that the respondents failed to prepare the said Electoral Roll accordingly, as such the present electoral roll should be declared illegal. He further submits that the Election Commission should be directed to take necessary assistance of modern and high-tech information technology in the preparation of electoral roll. The learned Advocate submits that to ensure a free, fair and credible election, the Election Commission must be independent of the executive. He then submits that as per Representation of the People Order, 1972 there are provisions for preparation of ballot boxes and that in the Electoral Roll Ordinance, 1982 there is provision for introduction of voter ID card which has been suspended by a subsequent Act and that as per section 30 of the Representation of the People Order, 1972 the Commission has the authority to revise such suspension by itself. Refer- ring some provisions of the Conduct of Election Rules, 1972, the learned Advocate submits that there are ample provisions regarding registration of political parties and the submission of return showing expenditure in election and that the Commission failed to follow the said law and Rules and that the Commission also failed to apply the Code of Conduct incorporated in 1996 resulting in some meaningless elections. The learned Advocate then submits that according to Article 126 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the Government is under legal obligation to assist the Election Commission for implementation of its objectives, namely, a free, fair and credible election. By referring Article 58 of the Constitution of the Republic, the learned Advocate submits that the present Caretaker Government, as such, is under legal obligation to provide all necessary assistances to the Election Commission to equip it with all, modern amenities before holding a free, fair and credible election and that the Caretaker Government should take necessary steps in consultation with the Election Commission for amending the necessary laws for achievement of the aforesaid purposes. 

 5. Mr Salahuddin Ahmed, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 and 3, finds it difficult to submit that Electoral Roll recently prepared is a flawless one. He however, submits that initiatives for revised roll have already been taken and that the respondents have been actively working for preparation of voter ID. 

 Articles 118 to 126 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh deal with provisions relates to the elections, formation, functions and steps to be taken by the Election Commission, the Electoral Roll, qualification, time of the election, validity of election laws and the effective assistance to Election Commission by the Government. To ensure free, fair and impartial elections, the Constitution declares that the Election Commission shall be independent in the exercise of its functions. Though the conditions of service of the Election Commissioners are to be determined by the President, in order to maintain their independence and freedom from political and executive influence, it is provided that an Election Commissioner can be removed only on the ground and in the manner a Judge of the Supreme Court may be removed. 

 8. The Constitution vests the power, superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for all the elections and conducts of such elections in. the Election Commission. The Commission is required to hold the presidential, parliamentary and other elections, delimit the constituencies of parliamentary elections and to prepare electoral rolls for the presidential, parliamentary and other elections in accordance with the Constitution and any other law passed by the parliament for the time being in this regard. Election is a long, elaborate and complicated process which starts with the notification for holding the elections and ends with the declaration of the result of polls in the manner prescribed by law. The Commission has to supervise, control and direct each and every step of the process to ensure free and fair election and the Commission must be deemed to have all the powers and discretion to ensure free and fair election as that is the manifest intendment of the Constitution in providing for the Commission. Parliament may by law regulate the exercise of the power of the Commission, but such a law has to be in conformity with the provisions of the Constitution of the Republic and it cannot in any way curtail or diminish the effectiveness of the Commission in holding free and fair elections. In exercise of the power, the Commission has two limitations namely, it must act in conformity with the Constitution and the laws validly made by Parliament and, like all other functionaries of the Republic, it must not act arbitrarily. 

 119. (1) The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for elections to the office of President and to Parliament and the conduct of such elections shall vest in the Election Commission which shall, in accordance with its Constitution and any other law" 

 11. Article 121 of the Constitution deals with a single Electoral Roll which runs as follows: 

 "There shall be one electoral roll for each constituency for the purpose of elections to Parliament and no special electoral roll shall be prepared so as to classify electors according to religion, race, caste or sex." 

 12. The High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 9157 and 9180 of 2005 discussed elaborately the manner of preparation of Electoral Roll by the Commission and directed the Election Commission to prepare the Electoral Roll in the following manner; 

 (i) It is held that the decision for preparation of Electoral Roll taken in the meeting on 6th August, 2005 was not the unilateral decision of the Chief Election Commissioner rather, it was a decision of the Commission for the preparation of the Electoral Roll and appointment of the Registration Officers, etc. 

 (iii) The Commission should prepare Electoral Roll taking the existing Roll maintained under section 7(6) of the Ordinance as a major basis. If there is a computerised database the Commission should make the best use of it and if not, a computerised Electoral Roll with database should always be maintained to avoid future controversy, costs and labour. 

 (iv) The persons whose names are already in the existing electoral roll cannot be dropped from that roll unless they are dead or have been declared to be of unsound mind or ceased to be residents or ceased to be deemed to be residents of that area or the constituency. 

 (v) The Chief Election Commissioner should immediately call a meeting of the Commission and the Commission should decide and take all appropriate steps to implement the decision of the Commission taken on 6th of August, 2005 in its meeting for preparation of Electoral Roll in the light of this judgment." 

 "III. The Commission should prepare Electoral Roll taking into consideration of the existing roll under section 7(6) of the Ordinance. If there is a computerised database the Commission should make the best use of it and if not, a Computerised Electoral Roll with data- base should always be maintained to avoid future controversy, costs and labour. 

 IV. The persons whose name are already in the existing Electoral Roll cannot be dropped from that Roll unless they are dead or have been declared to be of unsound mind or less than 18 years of age, ceased to be a citizen of Bangladesh or ceased to be deemed by law to be residents of the electoral area/constituency, the Commission if occasion arises for dropping the name from the existing Electoral Roll then shall do the same following the procedure as laid down in Sub-Rules (3) and (4) of the Rule 20 of the Electoral Rolls Rules, 1982." 

 15. So, the direction as given above by the Appellate Division is a mandatory one. On perusal of the aforesaid directions, the provision of Representation of the People Order 1972, Electoral Rolls Ordinance 1982, and Electoral Rules 1982, we are of the view that the Election Commission is under legal obligation as per Article 121 of the Constitution to prepare updated revised voter list strictly in compliance with the law as well as the directives given by the Appellate Division. It appears that the earlier Electoral Roll which is under challenge is a defective one as admitted by the high office of the Republic. Because of time constrain, the non co- operation of the political parties, political unrest in the country as well as for other reasons the then Election Commission failed to prepare an electoral role upto the mark. In such circumstances we are of the view that the respondents are under legal obligation to take immediate steps to prepare and upgrade the Electoral Roll in the light of the aforesaid observation made by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 54-55 of 2006 and they should take aid of the modem information technology such as introduction of Electoral Roll with photograph of the voters based on computerised data base. 

 20. Article 119 of the Constitution deals with the functions of the Election Commission. As per the said Article and other Articles in Chapter-VII of the-Constitution, the functions of Election Commission is to hold free, fair and neutral election in respect of any elected office of the Republic. The preamble of the Constitution, states that one of the basic features of the Constitution, is 'democracy' but it cannot be achieved without free, fair and credible election. As pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that there are sufficient laws already in existence, namely, the Representation of the People Order, 1972 and the Rules made thereunder, Electoral Roll Ordinance, 1982 and the Rules made thereunder, Conduct of Election Rules, 1972, Election Commission (registration of political parties) Rules, 2001, Code of Conduct as enacted by SRO/16/law dated 26-4-1996, etc. On perusal of the aforesaid laws, we find that there are ample provisions regarding the registration of political parties, eligibility of the candidates, election expenditure, related returns, different powers and functions of the Commission and the Code of Conduct which are preconditions for holding free and fair election. As per the provision laid down in Chapter-VII of the Constitution, we are of the view that it is the statutory duty of the Election Commission to follow and comply with the aforesaid provisions strictly during any election to be held under the Constitution. Considering the present context and development of the, 'school of democracy' and 'modem state' concept, we are of the view that the Election Commission should take all necessary steps in consultation with the present Caretaker Government to amend the relevant laws, so far as practicable for holding a free, fair and neutral election and to remove any future dispute in this regard to establish the true spirit of democracy. 

 21. In the affidavit-in-opposition, the learned Additional Attorney-General referred to Article IIE of the Electoral Rolls Ordinance, 1982 where a provision has been inserted for introduction of voter ID card though it appears that by a subsequent Act, namely Act XIII of 1996, the provision has been stayed. But Article 31 (8) of the Representation of the People Order 1972 runs as follows: 

 22. So it appears from the said amendment that though the said provisions for introduction of voter ID card is suspended for the time being the same can be revived by the Election Commission itself by notification in the official Gazette. It appears that the legislature conferred ample power upon the Election Commission to revive the said provision namely, Article 11 A of the Electoral Roll, 1982. In the present context of time, it appears that without any identification document, a free and fair election is impossible and election without an identification document now-a-days is neither desirable nor practicable. The spirit of the Constitution is to uphold the will of the people of the Republic and such reflection of the people will results in formation of a Government which is to be elected through a fair, free and credible election and conducted by the Election Commission. But it appears that because of different defects including non introduction of voter ID card most of the elections held after the liberation unfortunately, received question of fairness and neutrality. Considering the socioeconomic condition of the country, we are of the view that the Election Commission should take initiative to remove the existent legal barriers and introduce voter ID card or may introduce multipurpose national ID card with the assistance of the Caretaker Government because such documents are sine qua non for a credible election for a developing state. 

 24. As per the provisions of Articles 58(c) and 58(D)(2) of the Constitution, the present Caretaker Government is under the legal obligation to give all necessary assistance to the Election Commission to fulfill the objectives stated above and assistance is very much essential to implement the spirit of the preamble of the Constitution, Article 7 and Chapter- VII of the Constitution. It is impossible on the part of the Election Commission to achieve its goal without the co-operation from the Caretaker Government. The main function of the Caretaker Government is to assist the Election Commission to hold a free, fair and neutral election. The present Caretaker Government is under the legal obligation to assist the Election Commission in removing the existing defects to upgrade the obsolete method that presently exists and to introduce the most modem methods like preparation of Election Roll, identification document, namely, voter ID card/national ID card, modem ballot box, by amending all provisions of electoral laws in the present context. It is also the obligation to strengthen the Election Commission Secretariat and to allow it to function effectively and independently. 

 25. Article 123 of the Constitution of the Republic deals with the time for holding different elections. It appears that there is a provision for holding elections within a specified period. On perusal of the said Article, it appears that no consequence has been attached if the Election Commission fails to hold any election within the period prescribed in the aforesaid Article. It appears that though there is a provision for holding the Parliamentary Election within 90 days from the date of dissolution thereof but because of declaration of state of emergency as per under Article 141 A-C of the Constitution and suspension of the fundamental rights and other unavoidable circumstances, the Election Commission and Caretaker Government were not in a position to hold the elections within that period. The situation as prevailed at that time was beyond the control of the Election Commission and Caretaker Government and the main reasons for not holding of the election is the prevailing defects in the method of election over the years as pointed out by us earlier and non application of the existing election laws. The Election Commission is obviously under legal obligation to hold free, fair and credible election but we are of the view that such election can only be conducted by the Election Commission with the assistance of the present Caretaker Government after fulfilling the observation/directions given by us in the foregoing paragraphs.
